positive_evidence_found.note: The general predication form @ is defined in the official PTX ISA 9.3 control-flow section 9.7.13.2. Its Description states 'Execute an instruction or instruction block for threads that have the guard predicate True. Threads with a False guard predicate do nothing.' negative_evidence_notes: No clause using the words 'does not execute', 'not executed' (in a predication sense), 'no-op', or 'predicated off' was found in the official PTX ISA 9.3 HTML; the explicit false-guard wording used by the specification is 'do nothing'.

The words 'controls conditional execution' appear in sections 4.1 (line 1752), 5.4 (line 5340), and 9.3 (lines 7547-7548) without stating the false-guard state effect; the explicit state-effect statement is the section 9.7.13.2 clause.
predication_evidence_search.conclusion: Explicit false-guard no-op evidence exists in the official PTX ISA 9.3 general control-flow/predication section 9.7.13.2: 'Threads with a False guard predicate do nothing.' Combined with the general predicability rule 'All PTX instructions may be predicated' (PTX-9.3-MOV-016) and the guard-syntax rule of section 9.3 (PTX-9.3-MOV-021), this clause is the applicable official evidence for the guard-false behavior of predicated instructions, including mov.b32. Whether the semantic extractor classifies the mov.b32 guard-false consequence as a SOURCE_FACT on the basis of this general predication clause is a semantic-extraction decision; this bundle only records the evidence (GAP-1 status updated to RESOLVED_BY_SUPPLEMENT at the source level, with do_not_infer: true retained for curation).

mov.u64   d, fname;      // get address of device function

fragments.exact_quote:
Write register d with the value of a.
Operand a may be a register, special register, variable with optional offset in an addressable memory space, or function name.

fragments.section_heading: Data Movement and Conversion Instructions: mov
fragments.exact_quote:
For variables declared in .const, .global, .local, and .shared state spaces, mov places the non-generic address of the variable (i.e., the address of the variable in its state space) into the destination register. The generic address of a variable in const, global, local, or shared state space may be generated by first taking the address within the state space with mov and then converting it to a generic address using the cvta instruction; alternately, the generic address of a variable declared in const, global, local, or shared state space may be taken directly using the cvta instruction.
Note that if the address of a device function parameter is moved to a register, the parameter will be copied onto the stack and the address will be in the local state space.
fragments.reason_for_inclusion: Neighboring normative address semantics for the avar/avar+imm forms (out of the bounded base scope) and the device-function-parameter note; recorded for completeness of section 9.7.9.3.

fragments.section_heading: Data Movement and Conversion Instructions: mov
fragments.exact_quote:
Write scalar register d with the packed value of vector register a, or write vector register d with the unpacked values from scalar register a.
When destination operand d is a vector register, the sink symbol '_' may be used for one or more elements provided that at least one element is a scalar register.

fragments.exact_quote: All instructions have an optional guard predicate which controls conditional execution of the instruction. fragments.exact_quote: In PTX, the fundamental types reflect the native data types supported by the target architectures. A fundamental type specifies both a basic type and a size. Register variables are always of a fundamental type, and instructions operate on these types. The same type-size specifiers are used for both variable definitions and for typing instructions, so their names are intentionally short.

fragments.reason_for_inclusion: Fundamental type definition: a fundamental type specifies both a basic type and a size; register variables are always of a fundamental type; the same type-size specifiers are used for variable definitions and instruction typing.

fragments.exact_quote:
Most instructions have one or more type specifiers, needed to fully specify instruction behavior. Operand types and sizes are checked against instruction types for compatibility.
Two fundamental types are compatible if they have the same basic type and are the same size. Signed and unsigned integer types are compatible if they have the same size. The bit-size type is compatible with any fundamental type having the same size.
fragments.context_after: 3067-3068: In principle, all variables (aside from predicates) could be declared using only bit-size types...

fragments.exact_quote:
Registers (.reg state space) are fast storage locations. The number of registers is limited, and will vary from platform to platform. When the limit is exceeded, register variables will be spilled to memory, causing changes in performance. For each architecture, there is a recommended maximum number of registers to use (see the CUDA Programming Guide for details).
Registers may be typed (signed integer, unsigned integer, floating point, predicate) or untyped. Register size is restricted; aside from predicate registers which are 1-bit, scalar registers have a width of 8-, 16-, 32-, 64-, or 128-bits, and vector registers have a width of 16-, 32-, 64-, or 128-bits. The most common use of 8-bit registers is with ld, st, and cvt instructions, or as elements of vector tuples.
Registers differ from the other state spaces in that they are not fully addressable, i.e., it is not possible to refer to the address of a register. When compiling to use the Application Binary Interface (ABI), register variables are restricted to function scope and may not be declared at module scope. When compiling legacy PTX code (ISA versions prior to 3.0) containing module-scoped .reg variables, the compiler silently disables use of the ABI. Registers may have alignment boundaries required by multi-word loads and stores.
fragments.context_after: 2632: </section>; 2633: section heading 5.1.2. Special Register State Space
fragments.reason_for_inclusion: Register (.reg) state space: registers are fast storage; scalar register widths include 32-bit; predicate registers are 1-bit; registers are not fully addressable; declaration scope rules.

fragments.exact_quote: The special register (.sreg) state space holds predefined, platform-specific registers, such as grid, cluster, CTA, and thread parameters, clock counters, and performance monitoring registers. All special registers are predefined.
fragments.context_before: 2633-2636: section heading 5.1.2. Special Register State Space
fragments.reason_for_inclusion: Special register (.sreg) state space: holds predefined, platform-specific registers; this is the state space behind the out-of-scope sreg source category of scalar mov.

fragments.exact_quote:
All storage for data is specified with variable declarations. Every variable must reside in one of the state spaces enumerated in the previous section.
A variable declaration names the space in which the variable resides, its type and size, its name, an optional array size, an optional initializer, and an optional fixed address for the variable.
Predicate variables may only be declared in the register state space.
fragments.context_after: 3756: rubric: Examples (declaration examples .global .u32 loc; .reg .s32 i; .reg .pred p, q, r; etc.)
fragments.reason_for_inclusion: Variable declaration rules: a declaration names the state space, type and size, and name; predicate variables may only be declared in the register state space.

fragments.exact_quote:
Since PTX supports virtual registers, it is quite common for a compiler frontend to generate a large number of register names. Rather than require explicit declaration of every name, PTX supports a syntax for creating a set of variables having a common prefix string appended with integer suffixes.
For example, suppose a program uses a large number, say one hundred, of .b32 variables, named %r0, %r1, ..., %r99. These 100 register variables can be declared as follows:
.reg .b32 %r<100>;    // declare %r0, %r1, ..., %r99
This shorthand syntax may be used with any of the fundamental types and with any state space, and may be preceded by an alignment specifier. Array variables cannot be declared this way, nor are initializers permitted.
fragments.reason_for_inclusion: Register variable naming foundation: PTX supports virtual registers and parameterized variable names with any fundamental type (example .reg .b32 %r<100>;) and any state space.

The .f16 floating-point type is allowed in half precision floating point instructions and texture fetch instructions. The .f16x2 floating point type is allowed only in half precision floating point arithmetic instructions and texture fetch instructions.

This enables compiler optimization and ensures that the .param variable does not consume extra space in the caller’s frame beyond that needed by the ABI.
